content: CCR1, also known as C-C chemokine receptor type 1, is a protein encoded by the CCR1 gene in humans. This receptor has also been designated as CD191, which stands for cluster of differentiation 191. The CCR1 gene encodes a member of the beta chemokine receptor family, which is part of the G protein-coupled receptor superfamily. The ligands that bind to this receptor include CCL3 (also referred to as MIP-1 alpha), CCL5 (commonly known as RANTES), CCL7 (also called MCP-3), and CCL23 (referred to as MPIF-1). Chemokines and their receptors play a pivotal role in signal transduction processes, which are essential for recruiting effector immune cells to sites of inflammation. Studies involving knockout models of the mouse homolog of CCR1 have provided evidence for its roles in host defense mechanisms during inflammatory responses, as well as its involvement in susceptibility to viral and parasitic infections. Additionally, the CCR1 gene is part of a gene cluster located on chromosome 3p, which includes other chemokine receptor genes such as CCR2, CCRL2, CCR3, CCR5, and CXCR1. CCR1 has been demonstrated to interact specifically with the chemokine CCL5.
